Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model–rank configuration.

Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes fine-tuning large language models more accessible by learning a low-rank weight increment Δ ​ W = B ​ A \Delta W=BA while keeping pretrained weights fixed ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Its parameter efficiency depends on making effective use of a small number of trainable directions. The columns of B B define these directions in the output space, while A A contains their coordinates ( Zhu et al., 2024 ) . However, Park et al. (2025) observe that AdamW fine-tuning can produce highly correlated columns of B B , leading to basis redundancy and inefficient use of the available rank. They address this issue by imposing B ⊤ ​ B = I B^{\top}B=I , so that the basis is optimized on the Stiefel manifold. This constraint keeps the basis directions orthonormal while leaving their coordinates free to adapt. It preserves the class of representable rank-at-most- r r weight increments, as discussed in Section 2 .

Once the Stiefel constraint is imposed, a central algorithmic choice is how to maintain orthogonality during optimization. Stiefel-LoRA ( Park et al., 2025 ) enforces orthonormality through a retraction at each step. Landing methods ( Ablin & Peyré, 2022 ; Ablin et al., 2024 ) instead allow temporarily infeasible iterates and use an explicit correction to restore feasibility, avoiding per-step retractions. Manifold-LoRA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) applies this approach to LoRA fine-tuning. Beyond avoiding repeated retractions, allowing controlled departures from the manifold gives the optimizer additional freedom to explore the surrounding space. Figure 1 illustrates the potential benefit by comparing our proposed method (ProLand) with variants that replace its Landing correction with per-step retractions to enforce B ⊤ ​ B = I B^{\top}B=I . From the same initialization and under the same rule for computing product-space directions at their respective iterates, ProLand reaches a better stationary solution in this example. This observation motivates exploring infeasible paths while retaining control over constraint violation. Our goal is to improve the efficiency of this form of infeasible optimization for LoRA: make effective progress on the fine-tuning objective while rapidly recovering feasibility. These two goals are coupled, since an update that reduces the loss can also perturb the orthogonality of B B and interfere with the Landing correction. At the same time, the model depends on the joint weight increment B ​ A BA ; hence the directions chosen for the two factors should be coordinated. We introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that addresses these issues through two complementary design choices.

First, coordinated updates in the product space support rapid feasibility recovery. We design the joint first-order change D B ​ A + B ​ D A D_{B}A+BD_{A} in the represented weight increment and realize it through factor directions satisfying B ⊤ ​ D B = 0 B^{\top}D_{B}=0 , even when B B is infeasible. This condition makes the optimization step leave B ⊤ ​ B B^{\top}B unchanged to first order and eliminates its first-order interaction with the Landing correction. Consequently, the optimization step perturbs the constraint violation only at second order in its step size. Under the conditions of Section 4 , this violation contracts geometrically toward a neighborhood whose radius is quadratic in that step size. This provides a mechanism for recovering feasibility while continuing to optimize the represented weight increment. Second, Muon-style directions guide objective optimization. We incorporate the spectral update principle of Muon ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) into this coordinated construction. ProLand forms a momentum input in the space of realizable first-order changes in B ​ A BA , computes its polar factor, and projects the result back into that space. The spectral direction is therefore defined at the level of B ​ A BA , rather than independently in the two factor spaces, and is realized by the factor updates above while retaining their separation from feasibility restoration. This allows the spectral update and the Landing correction to be combined without a retraction at every step.

For the resulting method, we establish joint guarantees for objective stationarity and feasibility under suitable regularity and step-size conditions, assuming exact arithmetic. We show that the deterministic ProLand method attains O ( T − 1 / 2 ) O(T^{-1/2}) product-space stationarity and O ⁡ ( T − 1 ) O(T^{-1}) constraint violation at a randomized output. With stochastic gradients and horizon-dependent momentum and step size, the corresponding expected bounds are O ( T − 1 / 4 ) O(T^{-1/4}) and O ( T − 3 / 2 ) O(T^{-3/2}) . The constraint-violation bounds also hold uniformly along each trajectory after an initial transient. To make this construction practical for LoRA fine-tuning, we derive an exact low-rank implementation using momentum factors of width at most 2 ​ r 2r and polar-factor cores of size at most 2 ​ r × 2 ​ r 2r\times 2r , avoiding dense weight-sized optimizer states. In experiments, ProLand achieves the highest task-averaged scores among the compared methods on four GLUE tasks with DeBERTa-v3-base and across all tested decoder model–rank configurations. Matched ablations show that the Landing correction substantially reduces constraint violation.

Several methods improve LoRA optimization by coordinating the updates of its two factors. LoRA-Pro ( Wang et al., 2025 ) and LORO ( Mo et al., 2025 ) account for the change in the represented matrix when designing factor updates for fine-tuning and low-rank pretraining, respectively. LoRA-Muon ( Cesista et al., 2026 ) and sMuon ( Anson et al., 2026 ) extend Muon-style spectral optimization to low-rank adapters. In particular, sMuon reconstructs a low-rank gradient from factor gradients and derives coordinated directions through linearization and least squares, with momentum represented in factor coordinates. ProLand additionally imposes the Stiefel constraint on B B and selects a factor realization satisfying B ⊤ ​ D B = 0 B^{\top}D_{B}=0 at both feasible and infeasible iterates. This realization enables its spectral update to work with a separate feasibility correction. Spectral updates have also been developed explicitly for manifold optimization. Riemannion ( Bogachev et al., 2026 ) extends Muon to optimization of the represented matrix on the fixed-rank manifold. LoRA-TSD ( Andriianov et al., 2026 ) develops tangent-space spectral descent on that manifold and maps its updates back to the factors through a factor-induced retraction. Skewon ( Solonko et al., 2026 ) constructs spectral directions for a Stiefel-constrained matrix by solving a linear minimization problem over tangent directions subject to a spectral-norm constraint, followed by a retraction. These methods illustrate how spectral updates can be adapted to manifold geometry. ProLand focuses on the complementary challenge of combining such directions with infeasible iterates and controlled restoration of the basis constraint.

A complementary line of work avoids per-step retractions through Landing methods, which allow infeasible iterates and restore orthogonality through an explicit correction ( Ablin & Peyré, 2022 ; Ablin et al., 2024 ) . Manifold-LoRA ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) applies this approach to Stiefel and oblique constraints. Its update construction uses the gradient with respect to A A and a projected-gradient expression for B B , together with a feasibility correction; its analysis establishes convergence of the underlying retraction-free gradient method. ProLand retains the Landing mechanism and constructs its optimization direction in the space of joint changes in B ​ A BA . The resulting factor directions satisfy B ⊤ ​ D B = 0 B^{\top}D_{B}=0 even away from the manifold, eliminating all terms linear in the optimization step size from the recurrence for B ⊤ ​ B − I B^{\top}B-I . For this construction, we establish product-space stationarity guarantees and pathwise bounds on constraint violation under the conditions in Section 4 . Appendix F gives further comparisons.

We introduce ProLand, a retraction-free optimizer for LoRA with B B constrained to the Stiefel manifold; it combines product-level spectral updates with coordinated factor updates. The basis-factor direction has no first-order effect on the column orthonormality of B B , even at infeasible iterates, while a separate Landing correction progressively restores feasibility. An exact low-rank implementation avoids dense product-space optimizer states. Under the stated assumptions and step-size conditions, we establish deterministic and stochastic bounds on product-space stationarity and constraint violation at a common randomized output, assuming exact polar-factor computation. In the main language evaluations, ProLand achieves the highest task-averaged scores among the compared methods in the encoder setting and all seven decoder model–rank configurations. Matched ablations further show that Landing substantially reduces constraint violation.

chunks.section: Appendix A Product Geometry and Factor Realizations
chunks.text: This appendix collects the geometric results underlying the product-space formulation of ProLand. Section A.1 shows that the parameterization with B B constrained to the Stiefel manifold preserves the full rank-at-most- r r LoRA class and characterizes the first-order product space and its orthogonal projector. Section A.2 relates the projected gradient and product-space stationarity measure used in the convergence analysis to the first-order conditions of the factorized constrained problem. Section A.3 shows that every realizable product direction admits a factor realization satisfying the orthogonality condition required by the feasibility analysis, and establishes the reconstruction identity used by the exact low-rank implementation.

chunks.section: Empirical control of the B B spectrum.
chunks.text: We examine how Landing controls the spectrum of B B during Qwen2.5-3B fine-tuning on CodeAlpaca. We compare Landing strengths under linear-decay and constant learning-rate schedules, including the same update with Landing removed. Training settings are collected in Appendix L.4 . LoRA learns a weight increment Δ ​ W = B ​ A \Delta W=BA while keeping pretrained weights fixed ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Representative extensions modify rank allocation through AdaLoRA ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) , use different learning rates for the two factors through LoRA+ ( Hayou et al., 2024b ) , or separate weight magnitude and direction through DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . These developments address different aspects of low-rank adaptation. Expanding the discussion in Section 1.1 , we focus on methods that explicitly design the matrix update induced by the factors, impose geometric constraints on the adapter, or change how feasibility is maintained.

The product-space viewpoint concerns the represented matrix B ​ A BA , whose first-order variation is D B ​ A + B ​ D A D_{B}A+BD_{A} . LoRA-Pro selects factor gradients by matching this induced matrix direction to the full fine-tuning gradient in the Frobenius norm ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . LORO derives joint factor updates from Riemannian descent of the represented matrix for low-rank pretraining, combining periodic exact Riemannian updates with cheaper approximate factor updates ( Mo et al., 2025 ) . Spectral methods extend this viewpoint using Muon-style polar-factor directions ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . In particular, sMuon reconstructs a low-rank product-space gradient from factor gradients and derives factor directions by linearizing a relaxed Muon objective and solving the resulting least-squares problem ( Anson et al., 2026 ) . LoRA-TSD instead develops tangent-space spectral descent with a factor-induced realization ( Andriianov et al., 2026 ) . ProLand additionally constrains B B to the Stiefel manifold and realizes the projected product direction through coordinated factor updates. For the input J t J_{t} in Algorithm 1 , the selected product direction is ξ t = Π t ​ polar ⁡ ( J t ) \xi_{t}=\Pi_{t}\operatorname{polar}(J_{t}) , the Frobenius orthogonal projection of the polar factor onto the current space 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} of realizable first-order product variations. The coordinated factor directions realize this projected direction, rather than the unprojected polar factor; see Section 3 and Appendix A.3 .

The constraint may be imposed on the represented matrix or on its factors. Riemannion and LoRA-TSD optimize the represented update on the fixed-rank manifold ℳ r := { W ∈ ℝ m × n : rank ⁡ ( W ) = r } \mathcal{M}_{r}:=\{W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}:\operatorname{rank}(W)=r\} ( Bogachev et al., 2026 ; Andriianov et al., 2026 ) . Skewon addresses a different object: it solves a spectral-norm linear minimization problem over T X ​ St T_{X}\operatorname{St} for a supplied matrix direction, rather than constructing coordinated updates of a LoRA product ( Solonko et al., 2026 ) . Among factor-constrained methods, Stiefel-LoRA uses B ∈ St ⁡ ( m , r ) B\in\operatorname{St}(m,r) with A A unconstrained ( Park et al., 2025 ) , and Manifold-LoRA additionally considers an oblique constraint, which normalizes the columns of B B without requiring mutual orthogonality ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Two-sided formulations use three factors: StelLA writes U ​ S ​ V ⊤ USV^{\top} and PoLAR writes X ​ Θ ​ Y ⊤ X\Theta Y^{\top} , with two Stiefel basis factors and an unconstrained r × r r\times r core ( Li et al., 2025 ; Lion et al., 2025 ) . ProLand retains the two-factor representation B ​ A BA and constrains only B B . As shown in Section 2 , this formulation represents the full rank-at-most- r r class. This representational statement is separate from the convergence assumptions: under the regularity and safe-region conditions of Section 4 , the analyzed post-initialization products have rank r r . The distinction from direct fixed-rank optimization is therefore not simply an admissible-rank comparison, but the use of coordinated factor directions satisfying B ⊤ ​ D B = 0 B^{\top}D_{B}=0 while realizing a selected first-order product variation.

Feasibility treatment further distinguishes these approaches. Stiefel-LoRA uses a QR retraction on B B , whereas StelLA uses polar retractions on its two basis factors ( Park et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . Riemannion uses a truncated-SVD retraction of the represented matrix, and LoRA-TSD uses a factor-induced retraction on ℳ r \mathcal{M}_{r} ( Bogachev et al., 2026 ; Andriianov et al., 2026 ) ; these are rank constraints on the product, not orthogonality constraints on either LoRA factor. Skewon also uses a retraction to maintain feasibility of its Stiefel variable ( Solonko et al., 2026 ) . In contrast, Landing methods allow intermediate infeasible iterates and apply an explicit correction to recover feasibility ( Ablin & Peyré, 2022 ; Ablin et al., 2024 ) . Manifold-LoRA applies this mechanism to projected-gradient factor updates and establishes convergence for its SGD-type variant ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) ; PoLAR uses Landing fields on both basis factors in its practical fine-tuning algorithm ( Lion et al., 2025 ) . ProLand retains a separate Landing correction on B B , while exploiting the identity B t ⊤ ​ D B , t = 0 B_{t}^{\top}D_{B,t}=0 even at infeasible iterates. This identity eliminates the optimization-induced term linear in γ t \gamma_{t} and the mixed optimization–Landing term in the exact Gram recursion in Section 4 . The optimization step therefore contributes only a quadratic perturbation to that recurrence. Appendix C.1 gives the expansion and explains why the usual skew-symmetry condition on B ⊤ ​ D B B^{\top}D_{B} does not by itself eliminate the mixed term away from feasibility.

Momentum handling and low-rank computation are separate from the choice of feasibility mechanism. Riemannion uses projection transport to move tangent-vector momentum between successive tangent spaces ( Bogachev et al., 2026 ) . Skewon’s algorithms accept a supplied direction M t M_{t} , which may be a gradient or momentum, but do not prescribe a recursion for projecting or transporting a stored momentum state between those spaces ( Solonko et al., 2026 ) . ProLand explicitly reprojects its previous state before combining it with the current projected gradient; hence both the updated momentum H ¯ t \bar{H}_{t} and the polar-factor input J t J_{t} lie in 𝒮 t \mathcal{S}_{t} . This gives rank bounds of at most 2 ​ r 2r for both matrices. Reduced spectral computations already appear in sMuon and Skewon ( Anson et al., 2026 ; Solonko et al., 2026 ) ; ProLand’s implementation contribution is the exact low-rank realization of its complete projected-momentum and Landing iteration. Given an initial momentum factorization of width at most 2 ​ r 2r , Appendix B proves equivalence to Algorithm 1 in exact arithmetic, using factor gradients from the same sampled loss and a polar-factor core with at most 2 ​ r 2r rows and columns, without forming dense product-sized gradients or momentum states. chunks.text: Liu et al. (2025, Section 3.5, Table 6) cross Muon and AdamW between pretraining and full-parameter SFT using Moonlight checkpoints trained on 1.2T tokens. On their four reported benchmarks, Muon-pretrained checkpoints fine-tuned with Muon outperform the same checkpoints fine-tuned with AdamW. For low-rank adaptation, Anson et al. (2026, Section 4) explicitly hypothesize that Muon-based LoRA may perform better on Muon-pretrained Moonlight and report partial support across eleven tasks. They also identify Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B as AdamW-pretrained, which is the source of our backbone classification. Qu et al. (2026) study optimizer mismatch with controlled pretraining and fine-tuning experiments and find that LoRA can mitigate it by constraining updates. These findings motivate our choice of models pretrained with different optimizers. The Moonlight comparison in Table 4 uses the same pretrained checkpoint for all adapter methods.
